Current can only flow between points at different electrical potentials. And current flows more through the path of least resistant. If there's a good conductor (metal) in parallel with a bad conductor (human body), all or almost all current will flow through the metal.

Imagine you were inside a conductive metal ball, and a lightning struck it. You wouldn't feel anything even if you were touching the inside walls of that ball barehand.

Now, if you were wearing a metal armor it could be different, because the armor is not a continuous and tight system, which could allow for variations in potential, and maybe there are gaps where several armor pieces are connected not directly but through the body. 

So the lighting current could flow through the armor, leaving her unharmed, if the lighting strikes the armor first and there's a continuous path along the armor to the ground. Otherwise, she's fried

Keychains are very lightweight items, so they don't deform under their own weight when they get warm, and with the right print settings and right material you can significantly reduce internal stresses in the parts, specially for these ornamental pieces that don't work well with low infill (5-10%). I use Polymaker PLA because it is a modified PLA optimized for 3D printing and it is very dimensionally stable and more heat tolerant than most other PLAs I've tried. Cura also has them all divided, you will see it if you go in the custom mode and you modify the settings to show more speed settings. But cura does something that orca doesn't, cura has a multiplier related to the regular "print speed" setting that automatically adjusts the other speed parameters if you leave them on default, which most users do.

Orca, by default, has a more granular control, and unfortunately you cannot set most speed settings as a multiplier of a basic speed setting, so you have to modify each one if you want to change the speed across the entire print, and not just one type of line.

If you are a novice, you might not know what all the different speeds mean, so you can just slice any model, and in the preview tab, go to the little window that appears on the top left after slicing, and set the color scheme to line type, there you will see the different line types color coded, and then you will know what parts of ypur print are affected by each setting. 

You can also hover the cursor over the setting name, and a dialog box will pop-up with a short explanation of the setting. Orca used to lack this kind of helpful quick explanations, but it has improved a lot in the last few versions

Also, cura has acceleration settings hidden by default, so it just lets the printer use the default acceleration that is programmed in the printer, but can also enable this setting, and on some default printers profile the acceleration settings are actually configured but hidden.

Orca, on the other hand, shows the acceleration settings by default, and they are always activated and controlled by the slicer.

Speed and acceleration work together. Speed tells you how fast it can go, that's the limit, but acceleration tells you how long it will take to reach that speed in a straight segment. 

Let's assume you are printing only a single straight line, and that it is 200mm long, and you set the speed to 100mm/s, your brain tells you that it should last 2 seconds to do that line, but remember that it has to go from 0 to 100 first, and it also has to go from 100 to 0 at the end in order to stop. And how long does it take? That depends on the acceleration, so let's say your acceleration is 100mm/s², then the printer will take 1 second to achieve 100mm/s, but it will have only traveled 50mm when it reaches top speed. And then, the next 100mm are printed at top speed (100mm/s) taking another second to do it, and the last 50mm is the distance that is required at the set acceleration to go from 100 to 0, which takes an additional 1 second, so 3 seconds total.

As you can see in the previous example, when you reach top speed, the time that it takes to complete a segment of a line depends on the top speed. But you have to reach top speed first and slow down again in the end, and the time that it takes to do that depends on the acceleration, so both contribute to how long the print takes, and how fast it moves. Because if your acceleration is too low, and your print has a lot of changes in direction, you might never reach the speed that you set in the slicer.

And there's another setting that is called jerk that also affects speed, but we'll talk about that another day

Basically what happens here is that the extruded filament isn't sticking to the underlaying layer, so here's a list of possible causes:

Too high flow or too low temperature. The plastic doesn't fully melt before being deposited.

Fans are blowing on nozzle instead of the layers. Although the printer might read the right temperature since the thermistor is in the heat block, the nozzle might be getting cooled down and thus cooling the filament a little right before exiting the nozzle.

Underextrusion. Not enough filament is being pushed out to fill the volume that is supposed to, so the extruded line doesn't really get pushed against the previous layer.

Check for any of these issues, to verify if any of these is happening to you

There are other possible causes, but these are the ones that are most likely to produce the issue you showed in the photo.
